content: International professional societies, such as the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics, the International Confederation of Midwives, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, are actively involved in advancing maternal and newborn health initiatives. Collaborative efforts with the Norwegian Knowledge Centre for the Health Services aim to develop tools, including educational videos and other audiovisual materials, to support the creation of evidence-informed health policies based on the recommendations outlined in this guidance. Various meetings and events have served as platforms for disseminating this guidance. These include the Royal Tropical Institute in the Netherlands (May 30, 2012, Amsterdam), the USAID Community Health Worker Summit (June 2012, Washington, D.C.), the Family Planning Summit (July 11, 2012, London), the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Conference (October 7–12, 2012, Rome), the Canadian Network for Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health Annual Meeting (October 2012), the Second Global Symposium on Health Systems Research (October 31–November 3, 2012, Beijing), the East Central and Southern Africa Association of Obstetrical and Gynaecological Societies (ECSAOGS) Conference (2012, Maputo), the Maternal Health Task Force meeting (January 15–17, 2013, Arusha), the All India Congress of Obstetrics and Gynaecology (AICOG) (January 16–20, 2013, Mumbai), Women Deliver 2013 (May 28–30, 2013, Kuala Lumpur), and the French-Speaking Countries Summit 2013. Other dissemination activities include piloting the workbook (Annex 8) in various countries, utilizing web-based audiovisual platforms like YouTube to share clips and information about the guidance methods and recommendations, and engaging in community practice and discussion forums such as Afro-Nets. Dissemination efforts also involve the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia (SEARO) working group on human resources and task shifting, as well as potential support from USAID for derivative products to communicate recommendations to stakeholders. The recommendations in this guidance are intended for use in both international and national adaptation initiatives. Feedback received will be documented and utilized for future updates. Members of the WHO Technical Secretariat and researchers from the Norwegian Knowledge Centre for the Health Services are currently conducting user testing of the evidence-to-recommendation frameworks outlined in this guidance. This evaluation will contribute to future revisions of the guidance. The recommendations will be updated within five years (by 2018) unless significant new evidence emerges that necessitates earlier changes. The references cited include key resources such as the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2012), systematic reviews on task-shifting and health worker roles, and studies on maternal and newborn health interventions. These references provide a robust foundation for the evidence-based recommendations and strategies outlined in the guidance.
